title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
authors: Delip Rao, Ahmed Muharram, Chris Callison-Burch
abstract: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot

title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
authors: Alicia Colmenero-Fernández
abstract: Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. title: From Relevance to Validity: Zero-Shot Tool Selection via Functional and Contextual Validation
authors: Xiaoxuan Dong, Jin Zhang, Zichen Yuan et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly face tasks from unseen domains and execution contexts, making zero-shot tool selection essential for identifying tools that can satisfy task requirements. Existing dominant methods mainly rely on relevance ranking, but semantic matching alone cannot ensure that a tool is functionally compatible or remains applicable in a new context. title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
authors: Yuyao Ge, Shenghua Liu, Peizhong Gao et al.
abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside

title: CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval
authors: Xinyi Cheng, Tianfu Zhang, Jiwen Li et al.
abstract: Large language models increasingly generate multiple retrieval actions jointly, while downstream systems often provide only one reward for the resulting set. Broadcasting this reward provides a valid score-function gradient estimator for the expected set-level objective, but does not determine a coalition-dependent within-set attribution. title: EvalBuilder: Can LLMs Build Efficient Benchmarks?
authors: Huaisheng Zhu, Hangfan Zhang, Teng Xiao et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for long-horizon research and engineering, yet evaluating these capabilities remains expensive, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on human expertise. This motivates a natural question: can LLM agents themselves construct efficient benchmarks that preserve the conclusions of costly reference evaluations? title: Explorer-Zero: Improving Self-Play for Long-Horizon Tasks with Decomposable Verifiable Rewards
authors: Tianyu Liu, Davide Belli, Bence Major et al.
abstract: Training LLM agents on long-horizon interactive tasks with reinforcement learning typically relies on human-annotated tasks and reliable verification, both expensive to construct for stateful environments. Self-play offers an alternative, but must generate achievable, compositional tasks and provide feedback beyond binary outcomes. We propose Explorer-Zero, a self-play framework that jointly generates tasks and fine-grained, verifiable rewards through environment interaction. A learned proposer

title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery
authors: Qiuyu Chen, Qi Wang, Liang Xu et al.
abstract: Mathematical research drives scientific discovery, and recent advances in AI for mathematics have shown that language-model agents can solve challenging problems and develop substantial mathematical proofs. Yet much of today's AI-for-mathematics work centers on obtaining a final answer. title: ActionOPD: Distilling Decisions, Not Tokens
authors: Huining Yuan, Xiangmin Yi, Zelai Xu et al.
abstract: Distilling capable language-model agents into smaller models requires aligning the student's behavior with the teacher's. This raises a fundamental question: at which states and at what granularity should this alignment be performed? Offline imitation provides dense but token-specific supervision and can suffer from state-distribution mismatch. title: ReproBAIT: Can coding agents build their own biological AI tools?
authors: Shiv Muthupandiyan, Tolga H. Dur, Mac Walker et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly competent at leveraging scientific knowledge and existing computational tools to execute complex workflows. At present, little information exists on their ability to reconstruct tools when given limited descriptions of such tools. title: Evolve Together, Fall into Place: How Social Scaffolding Shapes Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Seojin Hwang, Youngmin Choi, Hwanhee Lee
abstract: Recent work lets LLM agents evolve their own harness, up to the team itself. Yet in human groups, the same abilities achieve different outcomes under different social conditions. Borrowing the notion of scaffolding from developmental psychology, we investigate whether the social scaffolding of a self-evolving multi-agent system (MAS), namely its team composition and structure of interdependence (e.g., collaboration, conformity, or competition), shapes how the team evolves. title: New Model, Old Habits: Behavior Transfer under Model Swapping in Multi-Session LLM Agents
authors: Youngbin Choi, Sehyun Hwang, Suhyeon Jun et al.
abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Bas

title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios
authors: Chenhao Yuan, Bohan Yu, Yinhao Xu et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly tackle complex real-world tasks in specialized domains. However, identifying and correctly applying domain-specific rules remains challenging when scenario information is distributed across multiple files. Existing rule-reasoning benchmarks typically represent scenarios using only a few factual statements, simplifying the identification and application of relevant rules. title: Interlock: From Local Correctness to Task Completion in Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Linji Hao, Yanji He, Zihan Wang et al.
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly undertake long-horizon tasks in complex environments characterized by fragmented evidence, partially completed states, and dependencies across resources and artifacts. Existing agents may satisfy individual requirements while failing to maintain these relationships, producing locally correct but incomplete outcomes. These failures arise because task completion depends on relationships among environmental evidence, consequential decisions, and required eff

title: MCAIR: Monitoring and Correcting Agent Unfaithfulness via Internal Representations
authors: Yan Xu, Dandan Song, Luan Zhang et al.
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in completing complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool interactions. However, recent studies have revealed that LLM-based agents can exhibit unfaithful behaviors, where their final reports fail to faithfully reflect their actual execution trajectories. title: Measuring and Reducing Unusable Replies of LLM Agents
authors: Yilin Jiang, Fei Tan, Xuanyu Yin et al.
abstract: People delegate multi-step work to LLM agents and read only the reply that the agent hands back. Current evaluation scores task completion and the faithfulness of reports, and it leaves open whether the requester can understand and use the reply. We call this property reply usability and measure it with a reader model that takes the requester's position and tests whether the reply can be interpreted from what the requester has seen, is in the requester's language and answers the request. title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents
authors: Maolin Ran, Minda Chen, Di Huang et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically t

title: J-tau: A Fully Localized Japanese Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
authors: Chihiro Yano, Jun Hirako, Hiroaki Yamagiwa et al.
abstract: We present J-tau, the first publicly available Japanese benchmark for evaluating tool-using LLM agents in interactive customer-support scenarios. While tau-bench is widely used to evaluate LLM agents, it is English-centric and cannot evaluate agents in other languages. Existing multilingual extensions offer no public Japanese version and rely primarily on machine translation, leaving locale-specific entities such as addresses and currencies inconsistent with the target region. To enable reliable

title: Divergent Paths: Learning an Outcome-Predictive Representation of LLM Agent Trajectories
authors: Alexander Gill, Guram Gogia, Francisco Guzmán
abstract: In this work, we reframe agentic trajectories as paths through a shared embedding space of actions and environmental observations. We show that successful and failed rollouts of the same task separate in this space, with simple per-task discriminators predicting held-out rollout outcomes at up to 0.95 AUROC across three agent benchmarks and three policy models. title: JockeyBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Horse-Racing Decision-Making
authors: Zhongwei Xie, Xingsu Li, Jingqiao Yu et al.
abstract: Repeated event forecasting requires extracting predictive signals from noisy evidence and evaluating their value across successive decisions. We introduce JockeyBench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol that studies this problem through historical Japanese horse racing. The protocol combines time-gated evidence, priced tools, paired frozen-program controls, and two workflows: executing an LLM-written predictor or acquiring evidence for a fresh per-race LLM forecast. title: XferAgent: Cross-Agent Experience Transfer for Self-Improving LLM Agents
authors: Weihao Li, Jun Bai, Shijie Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can reuse experience from prior task executions to improve performance on subsequent tasks. Although existing methods enable cross-agent experience sharing, differences in agents' execution histories and task requirements make shared experiences difficult to reuse effectively. We propose XferAgent, a framework for cross-agent experience transfer that organizes reusable experience in local and shared experience graphs. XferAgent reconciles compatible contribution

title: $τ$-Emotion-Bench: Exposing the Interaction Fragility of LLM Agents through Real-World User Emotions
authors: Rishitosh Kumar Singh, Amir Saeidi, Shamanthak Hegde et al.
abstract: In long-horizon tool-calling tasks, LLM agents can fail not only because of tool-use errors, but also because of ineffective interaction with users. Yet existing benchmarks largely assume cooperative and behaviorally stable users, leaving the effect of emotional variation on agent reliability underexplored. title: Retrieve What Helps, Only When It Helps: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Machine Translation
authors: Shijun Li, Yang Liu, Najmeh Sadoughi et al.
abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. title: Structure Before Intelligence: Gating What Agentic Scientific Workflows Release
authors: Ashish Acharya, Aman Al Amin, Hong Qin
abstract: An agentic scientific workflow can run to completion and still release wrong results: a silent numerical error, a stale input, or a defect in a shared upstream step can contaminate several outputs while a sibling branch stays correct. We treat trust in such results as a release decision. title: ActICL: Post-Training for Agentic Multimodal In-Context Learning
authors: Yanshu Li, Ruixiang Tang, Junyi Jessy Li et al.
abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. title: MemCode: Discrete Semantic Representations for Long-Term Agent Memory
authors: Xin Li, Liang Hu, Duoqian Miao et al.
abstract: Long-term memory remains a fundamental bottleneck for large language model (LLM) agents across sessions. Existing systems typically adopt a write-then-retrieve paradigm, storing context-dependent dialogue fragments and retrieving them via nearest-neighbor search in a continuous embedding space. This design yields unstable access units and systematically misses logically related but lexically distant evidence. We propose MemCode, a long-term agent memory framework that couples retrieval-oriented

title: EvoProbe: Evaluation-Driven Benchmark Evolution for LLM Agents
authors: Qianhong Guo, Wei Xie, Xiaofang Cai et al.
abstract: Static benchmarks for large language model (LLM) agents face saturation and data contamination risks, motivating continual updates to evaluation tasks. However, aggregate scores and success rates offer limited insight into specific problem-solving bottlenecks and provide limited guidance for subsequent task design. We propose EvoProbe, an evaluation-driven benchmark evolution framework that integrates task generation, diagnostic evaluation, and feedback-driven regeneration into a closed loop. It

title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
authors: Chenxu Wang, Xiaoyu Wen, Han Qi et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents accomplish complex tasks through multi-turn interactions with external tools. However, malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions. Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. title: STRATA: Self-Maintaining Structured Experience Graphs for Self-Evolving Language Agents
authors: Guanhua Zhu, Hanwen Li, Zhi Wei et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve at test time by accumulating experience: retrieving relevant memories before acting and writing new lessons back afterwards. Yet most are single-level: trajectories, distilled workflows and reasoning items all land in one undifferentiated pool indexed by embedding similarity, with no typed abstraction hierarchy. title: DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Tianle Chen, Pushkar Singh, Ketan Todi et al.
abstract: Language-model agents that run long tasks often redo work they have already done: they re-issue a tool call they made earlier and get back exactly the same observation, a step that adds no new information. We identify this failure as a loop. Loops appear natively in Qwen, Llama, and Gemini agents and become far more common once the agent's history is compressed to fit its context window. title: Beyond Corrected Actions: Training LLM Agents on Textual Critiques
authors: Thomas Zeng, Zelei Cheng, Mingyang Zhou et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. title: Where to Start, How to Move: Analyzing Curricula under GRPO for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
authors: Minchan Kim, Sungho Bae, Youngjin Kim et al.
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) provides no reward-relative learning signal when all rollouts receive identical rewards. In long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions, rewards are given only upon successful task completion, making all-fail groups common early in training and limiting opportunities to practice later steps. title: When Is Smaller Greener? Right-Sizing Language Models for Agentic AI
authors: Sajid Siraj, Maria Barbati
abstract: AI agents use large language models (LLMs) to plan and act over multiple steps, yet models are usually compared per call rather than per completed task. This paper asks: which model should an agent use to complete tasks reliably while minimising energy, cost and time? We show that per-call comparisons can be misleading for agentic AI. title: P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
authors: Mohsen Iranmanesh, Sina Moradi Sabet, Sina Marefat et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it -- a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. title: Function-Space Temporal Self-Distillation for Policy Optimization
authors: Aryan Das, Arnab Bhattacharya, Vinay Kumar Verma
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness
authors: Zihao Lin, Haoyu Dong, Haobo Xu et al.
abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We f

title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
authors: Jiatong Li, Yatao Bian
abstract: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. title: From Triage to Impact: A Multi-Hop Reasoning Benchmark for Explainable Persian Hate Speech
authors: Ghazal Kalhor, Sima Kamandloo, Mehrsa Shamsian et al.
abstract: Hate speech has become increasingly prevalent on social media, raising concerns about its detection, interpretation, and moderation. Persian, a relatively low-resource language, lacks sufficient annotated data and computational resources for fine-grained hate speech analysis. title: Argument Graph Uncertainty: Quantifying Uncertainty from the Logical Structure of Reasoning Chains
authors: Simon Baur, Sumire Honda, Wojciech Samek et al.
abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is essential for deploying large language models in high-stakes reasoning tasks, yet most existing approaches rely on expensive sampling strategies or shallow token-level signals that ignore the internal logical structure of model outputs. title: Scaling Multilingual Safety and Reasoning Evaluation through Reasoning-Guided Translation
authors: Zahraa Al Sahili, Ioannis Patras, Matthew Purver
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across languages, yet their safety and reasoning capabilities remain predominantly evaluated in English. Translating existing benchmarks offers a scalable approach to multilingual evaluation, but preserving task-specific meaning across languages presents significant challenges, particularly for harmful requests, mathematical reasoning, and conversational interactions. title: Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
authors: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Tong Lei et al.
abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. title: FACES: Fine-grained Gated Semantic Alignment for Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation
authors: Hang Ren, Peidong Wang, Yichen Gao et al.
abstract: In recent years, with advances in multimodal interaction technologies and the growing demand for intelligent emotional support, Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation (MESC) has emerged as an important task. However, existing systems still suffer from shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies due to weak semantic feedback, cross-dimension reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision. title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges
authors: Sebastian Nagl
abstract: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning
authors: Jiangcheng Song, Haodong Jing, Yulin Mu et al.
abstract: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification

title: Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
authors: Fiorenzo Parascandolo, Enver Sangineto, Xiaoyi Yu et al.
abstract: Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. title: Rationale Distribution Distillation via Flow Matching for Distributional Continuous Latent Reasoning
authors: Mingyeong Kim, Gyusang Cho, Juho Lee et al.
abstract: Sampling multiple chain-of-thought rationales from a language model can uncover correct solutions missed by a single attempt. However, these rationales are typically lengthy, making repeated autoregressive generation costly. Continuous latent reasoning offers a compact alternative, but point-valued methods condition repeated answer sampling on a single rationale, which can limit exploration of diverse paths and answer coverage. title: SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets
authors: Yixian Tan, Aulia Adila, Jonathan Heng et al.
abstract: We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages (Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil) on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. title: Learning Perception to Action Rules through Reinforcement Learning for Theory-of-Mind Reasoning
authors: Soyoung Oh, Nursulu Sagimbayeva, Nicholas Jennings et al.
abstract: In Theory-of-Mind (ToM) reasoning, large language models may correctly infer the agent's mental state but fail to use that inference when predicting or judging the agent's subsequent actions. In this work, we investigate whether explicitly connecting perception, belief, and action with rules improves ToM reasoning. title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla
authors: Md Rayhanul Masud, S M Maksudul Alam, Mohammad Jaminur Islam
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
authors: Xiaocong Yang, Xuanyu Meng, Yuji Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specif

title: PN-Mix: Pair-Norm Guided Mixed-Precision Key Cache Quantization for Efficient Long-Output LLM Inference
authors: Gil Jae Song, Sungjoo Yoo
abstract: Long-output inference in large language models suffers from severe KV cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. While KV cache quantization alleviates this issue, low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) severely degrades model accuracy. Recent mixed-precision key-cache quantization methods mitigate this degradation by allocating higher precision to important key channels, but estimate channel saliency using only key statistics. title: Who's Behind the Text? Robust Model Authorship Attribution
authors: Minseok Ko, Hyunseok Lee, Woomin Song et al.
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate text, their misuse has become a growing societal problem, with implications for academic misconduct, model distillation, and cyberattacks. For these reasons, Model Authorship Attribution (MAA), which identifies the source model of a given text, is important for promoting the responsible use of LLMs and improving AI safety. title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone
authors: Kutay Tire, Atula Tejaswi, Haris Vikalo et al.
abstract: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous "soft-token" representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. title: Integrating Simulation and Chain-of-thought Reasoning in Multimodal-Language Models For Physical Reasoning
authors: YingQiao Wang, Eric Bigelow, Tomer Ullman et al.
abstract: Multimodal language models often need to reason about the physical dynamics of the world in order to answer questions appropriately. Various methods have emerged for solving physical reasoning tasks, and in particular, two leading approaches are Chain-of-Thought reasoning and physics-grounded simulation. title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
authors: Shuyuan Zheng, Yun-seo Lee, Xing Gao et al.
abstract: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Zhaoyan Jia, Chengwei Zhou, Gourav Datta et al.
abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. title: Cortex: Consolidating Context into Parametric Memory
authors: Jintian Zhang, Feng He, Xinnian Liang et al.
abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. title: Beyond Static Cues: Unified Dynamic Detection of MLLM Backdoors via Dual-Flow Trajectory Analysis
authors: Yinzhen Huang, Jiahe Xie, Yitong Sun et al.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, yet their susceptibility to backdoor attacks remains a formidable challenge. While existing defenses have evolved from visual-centric patch cues to unsupervised internal attention statistics, they are fundamentally constrained by a reliance on static snapshots and attack-specific heuristics. title: Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
authors: Taha Sabir, Alberto Montero Molina, Thinh Quang Ly et al.
abstract: Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs
authors: Oscar Chew, Po-Yi Lu, Yi-Jie Cheng et al.
abstract: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. title: Manacá-1B-Instruct-2: Reproducible Safety Alignment for a Native Brazilian-Portuguese LLM. Negative DPO Results, a Controlled Composition Scan, and a Silent Failure Mode of the LLM Judge
authors: Bruno Leonardo Santos Menezes, Carlos Leonardo Souza Cardoso, Fabio André Machado Porto
abstract: Brazilian Portuguese remains underserved by open-source language models, and the few that are safety-aligned rarely document what did not work or validate comparisons with statistical significance. We present Manacá-1B-Instruct-2, the second-generation post-training alignment of Manacá-1B (1.72B parameters, trained from scratch for PT-BR), with an SFT corpus of 291,223 examples. title: ChronoCulture: Evaluating Cultural Awareness Across Time in Large Language Models
authors: Rusali Saha, Nitya Khurana, Ruihong Huang et al.
abstract: Cultural attitudes and social norms evolve over time, yet most cultural benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) treat culture as a static attribute of a country or region. We introduce ChronoCulture, a benchmark of 10,360 temporal pairs built from longitudinal survey data across 72 countries. Each pair contains the same survey question asked in the same country in an older and a newer year, with full population response distributions as ground truth. title: Equal CER, Unequal Damage: Severity-Weighted Character Error Rate for OCR
authors: Nguyen Nguyen, Yongyi Zang
abstract: Character Error Rate (CER), the standard metric for OCR and vision-language models (VLMs), charges a typo as much as a wrong name. We introduce semCER, which keeps CER's alignment and denominator and charges each grapheme edit a severity from an LLM judge, with no word segmentation. Normalized CER keeps the score of a whole transcription, where it tracks readers as well as semCER or better, and semCER breaks that score down into named edits. title: Model vs. User: Whose Values Prevail? Inference-Time Value Alignment in Multi-Turn Conversations
authors: Enrico Liscio, Anne Arzberger, Aditya Shankar et al.
abstract: Human values shape how we expect language models to behave. Dominant alignment approaches treat values as global objectives, although the appropriate value orientation is personal and contextual. Training-free alignment can steer models toward target values at inference time, yet has been largely evaluated in single-turn settings and with a single steering direction (e.g., toward safety). title: Recognition Is Not Grounding: Benchmarking Multilingual Financial Evidence Extraction
authors: Lingfei Qian, Yan Wang, Xueqing Peng et al.
abstract: Comparing financial disclosures across languages requires identifying shared accounting concepts and recovering all numerical facts that express them. Existing benchmarks evaluate aspects of these capabilities, but provide limited insight into whether both succeed on the same multilingual evidence. In particular, it remains unclear whether language models can recognize these concepts across languages and exhaustively recover their corresponding numerical evidence from the same contexts. title: DANGERLENS: Probing Dangerous Representations Hidden by Safety Alignment
authors: Tianzhuo Yang, Shaoheng Yan, Lin Lu et al.
abstract: Safety alignment teaches language models to refuse harmful requests, yet the internal accessibility of hazardous concepts can retain traces of earlier training. Can checkpoints with equally safe behavior differ in what remains accessible behind their refusals? In this work, we investigate this question through paired training histories and a direct audit of intermediate representations. title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs' Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios
authors: Ali Zamani, Soroush Esfahanian, Erfan Shahabi et al.
abstract: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others' mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play

title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models
authors: Bohan Sun, Zunhai Su, Xialie Zhuang et al.
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. title: Quantifying privacy risks in foundation model representations of brain MRI
authors: Imen Bajar, Héber Hwang Arcolezi, Antoine Boutet et al.
abstract: Pretrained representations are increasingly used to share and reuse information from medical images without exposing the original scans, but it is unclear how much patient-specific information these representations retain. We investigate this question for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) by evaluating five frozen pretrained encoders spanning different architectures, pretraining objectives, and training domains on two longitudinal T1-weighted datasets, OASIS-2 and MIRIAD. title: OrionMoE-v1.0: A Mixture-of-Experts Foundation Model for Tabular In-Context Learning
authors: Mohamed Bouadi, Nassim Bouarour, Aditya Tanna et al.
abstract: Tabular foundation models enable in-context learning by predicting unseen observations from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates. Despite recent advances, most existing approaches rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations across features and datasets. We introduce OrionMoE-Small, a compact tabular foundation model that combines distribution-aware representations with dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts computation. title: From Unreliable to Usable: Decomposing Failure Modes and Confidence Signals in LLM Entity Extraction - Evidence from Cyber Threat Intelligence
authors: Jiahong Qian
abstract: Audits of large language model (LLM) extraction from full-length documents report severe unreliability, leaving two questions open: what the failures actually consist of, and whether confidence signals can turn unreliable output into usable output. We run a preregistered, fully frozen evaluation of two new-generation low-cost LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash) with a flagship-tier control (GPT-6.1-Sol) on a public corpus of 354 incident campaigns (315 unique reports, 630 model-report evalua

title: When Does Momentum Help in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards?
authors: Kaifei Wang, Zikang Shan, Liwei Wang et al.
abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $β$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. title: CSWBench: Evaluating Context-Sensitive Code-Switching in Creative Writing
authors: Zewen Jiang, Yahan Li, Chenlu Guo et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated multilingual capabilities across diverse language generation and understanding tasks. Yet effective code-switching requires more than multilingual proficiency: models must decide when, where, and why to switch languages in ways that fit the surrounding context. title: Drivers of LLM Consensus Formation Under Competing Incentives: A Simulation Study
authors: Isabel Jones, Matthew Edwards, Janina A. Hoffmann
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments that produce unanimous agreement, both in intended interactions that need coordination and in unintended emergent interactions. Consequently, understanding how LLMs with competing incentives reach consensus is crucial to better interpret and design LLM collectives. title: Which Knowledge Should LLMs Trust? Uncovering a Generalizable Steering Direction Across Knowledge Conflicts
authors: Yibin Lou, Yi Hu, Jianhui Chen et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model's residual stream. title: Gray-Box Hallucination Detection in LLMs with Token Identities
authors: Shaked Goldshtein, Yitzchak Grunbaum, Fabrizio Frasca et al.
abstract: Large language models often produce fluent but factually incorrect output. Gray-box detectors identify such hallucinations from the token-probability statistics emitted during generation, avoiding the need for white-box access to hidden states that frontier models do not provide. These detectors, however, typically rely only on probability-derived representations and ignore the identities of the candidate tokens. title: Safe-FCL: Continual Risk Awareness and Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation for Federated Continual Learning of LLMs
authors: Shuaijie Ma, Yongkang Hu, Yu Cheng et al.
abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables large language models (LLMs) to learn collaboratively from distributed client data, but malicious client updates can compromise global model safety. As federated tasks evolve, changing malicious update patterns challenge the ability of existing defenses to maintain reliable risk detection over time. title: When Protection Overrides Consequences: Understanding Protection Mode in Large Language Model Decision-Making
authors: Yuanfan Li, Junyi Chen, Qi Zhou et al.
abstract: Frontier language models excel at complex tasks yet may prioritize protection over larger physical consequences in simple, urgent decisions. GPT-5.6 Sol, for example, moves a girl playing in shallow water before retrieving a submerged camera. We call this Protection Mode and study it with ProtectionBench: 285 prompts, 34 physical families, and nine models. title: Not All Criteria Matter: Importance-Aware Criteria Weighting for Rubric-Based LLM Evaluation
authors: Haocheng Yang, Licheng Pan, Yiming Dong et al.
abstract: Rubric-based evaluation assesses the responses of large language models (LLMs) by aggregating the verification results of explicit criteria, yet not all criteria matter equally. However, existing methods commonly aggregate the verification results with uniform weighting, which assigns minor and overlapping criteria the same weight as essential ones and thus produces misleading evaluation scores. title: OpenTWBench (Open Taiwan Benchmark): Taiwan-Domain Knowledge Evaluation for Large Language Models, and How the Measurement Apparatus Shapes the Score
authors: Liang-Hsun Huang, Min-Yi Chen, Chao-Chun Chuang et al.
abstract: We present OpenTWBench, an open evaluation suite for Taiwan-domain knowledge in large language models, built around two benchmarks. tw-exam-bench contains 255,854 four-option questions across 148 academic subjects, from fifteen years of Taiwan's national examinations published as open data by the Ministry of Examination; answer keys agree across 31,312 duplicated question groups at 99.91%, with all 27 disagreements accounted for. title: Mitigating Video Hallucinations via Attention-Guided Representation Perturbation
authors: Zhixin Cai, Ruoqi Yuan, Xinchen Yang et al.
abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. title: C3: Rethinking Process Supervision via Confidence-Guided Credit Correction in Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
authors: Ai Jian, Haoran Pan, Eryu Guo et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly trained as multi-turn agents that interact with external tools. However, outcome-only reinforcement learning can produce a form of misguided reinforcement: even on successful trajectories, undesirable local behaviors may receive positive token-level advantages and be favored by the policy update. title: ReFormBench: Benchmarking the Stability of Response-Conditioned Format Correction in Large Language Models
authors: Tianxiang Gao, Yahan Li, Chenlu Guo et al.
abstract: Reliable use of large language models requires responses to satisfy formatting requirements across changing instructions. Standard compliance scores do not distinguish preserving a model's observed format from correcting it, or reveal whether that correction holds across variants. We introduce ReFormBench, a benchmark that uses each model's unconstrained response to the same question as its formatting baseline. title: HACHIMI-II: From Role-Play to Learner Behavior Modeling for Faithful Student Simulation
authors: Yilin Jiang, Fei Tan, Xuanyu Yin et al.
abstract: Simulated students let researchers test tutoring systems and teaching strategies before real learners are available, but only if the simulation reproduces where a particular learner succeeds and fails. The common approach asks a large language model to role-play a student, but a role does not model what this learner knows or will do next, so the model's own competence fills the gap. title: Twenty Days Later: A Pre-Registered Test of History-Based Forecasts of Brand Mentions in Gemini Answers
authors: Dmitrij Żatuchin
abstract: Counts of which brands a large language model names are useful only if they hold long enough to act on. We test this with a pre-registered replication. The same 162 requests (54 questions in English, Estonian and Finnish about three software categories, four of twelve candidate brands per question, three repeats) were sent to gemini-3.1-pro-preview in three waves within about ten hours on 22 and 23 September 2026, and again on 13 October 2026, 20.3 days after the third wave, with identical reque

title: Moral Combat: Exploiting Moral Foundations Theory to Jailbreak LLMs
authors: Adel Khorramrouz, Yi-Chia Wang, Sharon Levy
abstract: Social psychology has long described how people can be persuaded to interpret a harmful act as moral. Recent research suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) echo aspects of human psychology, from cognitive biases to social conformity. This raises a question with direct safety implications: can LLMs be moralized to bypass safety guardrails? title: TEX-MEX: Similarity-Guided Temporal Contrastive Learning for Time Series
authors: Aditya Radhakrishnan, Maxwell A. Xu, Wanting Mao et al.
abstract: Contrastive learning for time series depends on deciding which pairs of inputs should be treated as similar and dissimilar. Because few augmentations reliably preserve meaning in time series, prior methods have relied on two disjoint notions of similarity between windows: structural similarity, which relates windows with similar morphology, and temporal similarity, which relates windows that occur close together in time. title: Typed Decision Models on Tabular Data
authors: Baowen Zhang, Hangting Ye, Hongyuan Zha
abstract: Typed decision models are language models that answer a question with a fixed set of possible answers by returning a probability for each answer instead of generating text. We study them on tabular data and compare four decision models with three large language models (LLMs) on row classification, fact verification and anomaly detection. title: Structure-Preserving Document-Level Data Augmentation via Discourse Parsing
authors: Ruilin Shang, Shilong Hou, Zi Long et al.
abstract: Data augmentation (DA) plays a vital role in improving model performance in low-resource or limited-supervision scenarios within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Existing DA methods, such as synonym replacement and back-translation, have demonstrated effectiveness on the word or sentence level; however, they frequently neglect discourse-level coherence and logical flow, which are essential for complex tasks dependent on inter-sentential relationships. title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
authors: Javad Mirzaei, Jeebak Mitra
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). title: KoAGE: Do Large Language Models Know, Learn, and Coin Korean Neologisms?
authors: SungHo Kim, Eojin Jeon, SangKeun Lee
abstract: Korean neologisms arise through diverse mechanisms, a demanding test of language models beyond lexical memorization. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce NeoTrace, an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres. title: Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N Sampling for Verifiable Problems
authors: Taro Yano, Yoichi Ishibashi, Masafumi Oyamada
abstract: Best-of-N sampling is a simple inference-time scaling strategy for large language models, yet its behavior under incomplete reward models remains poorly understood. We study Best-of-N as a competition between the extreme reward tails of correct and incorrect responses. This view shows that success depends not only on the probability of sampling a correct response, but also on whether correct responses dominate incorrect ones in the upper tail. title: Can We Believe AI Peer Review?
authors: Zongrui Yang, Haoyuan Li, Zhongsheng Wang et al.
abstract: As large language models become widely used in scientific review and manuscript revision, AI scores are increasingly serving as feedback for assessing paper quality and guiding edits. Yet whether a single AI score reliably reflects the reviewer's judgment, and whether revision gains based on that score are endorsed by other reviewers, remain understudied. title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report
authors: LLM-jp,  :, Chaoran Liu et al.
abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
authors: Matthew Raffel, Lizhong Chen, Sai Munikoti et al.
abstract: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. title: Qwen-MT-Lumen at WMT2026: Instruction-Specialized Translation via Quality-Aware Training and On-Policy Distillation
authors: Hao Wang, Yangyang Liu, Xiaohu Zhao et al.
abstract: We present Lumen, The open-source model is available at, our submission to the WMT 2026 General Machine Translation Shared Task. We focus on instruction-specialized translation, where systems must produce accurate translations while satisfying fine-grained requirements on style, terminology, and structured output. title: Hindsight-Privileged RLVR: Single-Rollout Token Credit Without Group Sampling
authors: Wei Chen, Yubing Wu, Zhou Xu et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models from checked task outcomes, but assigning a terminal reward to individual reasoning tokens or actions remains difficult. Group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) sample several attempts per prompt, but lose their reward-based learning signal when all attempts receive the same outcome. title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
authors: Ian Magnusson, Noah A. Smith, Pang Wei Koh
abstract: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. title: Beyond Expert Rankings: Contrast Calibration for Mixed-Precision MoE Quantization
authors: Renjie Xie, Juncheng Yang, Aoting Hu et al.
abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models activate only a few experts per token, yet all expert weights must be stored. Mixed-precision quantization reduces this storage cost by assigning higher bit-widths to sensitive experts and lower bit-widths to resilient ones, but expert rankings alone do not determine how strongly to weight their errors. title: TreeFlex: Agents Navigating Their Own Search Trees
authors: Dongzhuo Li, Fangzhou Cheng, Weiwei Li et al.
abstract: A ReAct-style agent accumulates observations, intermediate results, and failed attempts in a single context. As this context grows, stale and off-path information consumes its limited capacity and obscures relevant evidence, making focused reasoning increasingly difficult. We introduce TreeFlex, a framework in which the agent's own policy decides where to search.
